content: Atypical pneumonia is a type of lung infection caused by specific bacteria, including Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydophila pneumoniae. Pneumonia itself refers to an infection that affects the lungs. Symptoms of Atypical Pneumonia Pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma and Chlamydophila bacteria is generally mild. However, pneumonia due to Legionella pneumophila tends to worsen over the first 4–6 days before gradually improving over the next 4–5 days. Even though symptoms may improve, complete resolution can take some time. The most common symptoms of pneumonia include: Chills. Cough, which may produce bloody mucus in cases of Legionella pneumonia. Fever, which can range from mild to high. Shortness of breath, which may only occur during physical exertion, such as climbing stairs. Other symptoms may include: Chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing. Confusion, particularly in older adults or those with Legionella pneumonia. Headache. Loss of appetite, low energy, and fatigue. Muscle aches and joint stiffness. Sweating and clammy skin. Less common symptoms include: Diarrhea, especially with Legionella pneumonia. Ear pain, eye pain, or soreness, particularly with Mycoplasma pneumonia. Neck lumps, rash, or sore throat, which are also associated with Mycoplasma pneumonia. Causes of Atypical Pneumonia Mycoplasma pneumonia is a type of atypical pneumonia caused by the bacterium M. pneumoniae. It typically affects individuals under the age of 40. Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia-related bacteria occurs year-round and accounts for 5–15% of all pneumonia cases. It is usually mild. Pneumonia due to Legionella is more common in middle-aged and older adults, smokers, and individuals with chronic illnesses or weakened immune systems. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care You should contact your healthcare provider if you develop a fever, cough, or shortness of breath. These symptoms can have various causes, and your doctor will need to rule out pneumonia. Diagnosis A thorough medical evaluation is necessary for individuals suspected of having pneumonia. It can be challenging to differentiate pneumonia from bronchitis, so a chest X-ray may be required. Depending on the severity of the illness, additional tests may include: Complete blood count (CBC). Blood cultures. Blood tests to identify the causative bacteria. Sputum culture. Urine tests or throat swabs. CT scan of the chest. Bronchoscopy (rarely needed). Open lung biopsy (only in severe cases where other diagnostic methods fail). Treatment Options At-home care steps include: Managing fever with aspirin, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen or naproxen), or acetaminophen. Avoid giving aspirin to children. Avoiding cough medicines unless advised by your doctor, as they may hinder the body’s ability to expel sputum. Drinking plenty of fluids to loosen secretions and help expel phlegm. Getting ample rest and delegating household chores to others. Antibiotics are the primary treatment for atypical pneumonia: Many patients can take oral antibiotics at home. Severe cases may require hospitalization, where antibiotics are administered intravenously, along with oxygen therapy. Antibiotics are typically prescribed for at least two weeks or longer. Common antibiotics used to treat atypical pneumonia include: Azithromycin. Clarithromycin. Erythromycin. Fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin). Tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline). Prognosis Most patients with pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma or Chlamydophila respond well to appropriate antibiotic therapy. However, Legionella pneumonia can be more severe and may lead to complications such as kidney failure, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), immune system weakness, or even death. Possible Complications Infections of the brain and nervous system, such as meningitis, myelitis, or encephalitis. Hemolytic anemia, a condition where the body destroys red blood cells faster than they can be replaced. Severe lung damage. Prevention Wash your hands frequently and encourage others around you to do the same. If you have a weakened immune system, avoid crowded places. Ask visitors with colds to wear masks. Get an annual flu shot. Consult your doctor about whether you need a pneumonia vaccine.
